source.title: AutoInterpretation Finds Sparse Coding Beats Alternatives

record.file_problem: The post text is intact, but the referenced figures are not rendered, so their plotted values cannot be read.
record.tranche_reason: It applies sparse coding and automatic interpretation to Pythia70M language-model activations and reports results relevant to indirect evidence for distributed or dictionary-recoverable features in LLMs. It does not reproduce the toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The study measures automatic-interpretation scores for sparse-coding features and comparison directions, rather than measuring superposition geometry, feature sparsity, or capacity directly. The post describes several comparisons qualitatively, but the plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text. Method descriptions and choices such as dictionary size are not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: It applies sparse dictionary learning to Pythia70M activations (MLP layer 1, residual layer 2). It measures whether the recovered directions are more interpretable than neuron-basis, random, PCA and ICA directions. That bears on V4, whether LLMs contain sparse features a dictionary can recover. It does not reproduce the toy-model experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in both MLP layer 1 and residual layer 2 of Pythia70M, sparse coding gives features more interpretable than all tested baselines (neuron basis, random, PCA, ICA), even without the learned bias. They say the residual-stream combined-score null result is misleading. They read this as evidence that networks use distributed linear features weakly anchored to the neuron basis. They call the results preliminary, based on a single MLP dictionary.
record.recipe_differences: The cited toy-model work studies superposition in toy networks; this post applies sparse coding and GPT-based automatic interpretation to Pythia70M activations. It does not measure feature overlap geometry or a sparsity transition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with layer (MLP versus residual stream), scoring set (top-and-random versus top-only or random-only), feature bias, and selection of high-MCS residual-stream features.

fits_no_version.finding: In the residual stream, neuron-basis directions beat random directions strongly in combined scoring. This is due to fragment-scale features that are somewhat neuron-aligned.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The residual stream contains partly neuron-aligned, fragment-level directions despite lacking a privileged basis.

fits_no_version.finding: Features found almost identically by two dictionaries (top_mcs) score higher than other learned features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary features that replicate across training runs are more interpretable.

record.problems: The authors describe the results as preliminary and note that only the first and so far only MLP sparse-coding dictionary had been tested. Feature counts varied between 40 and 150, and the supplied text lacks the plotted numerical values, preventing assessment of score magnitudes and confidence intervals. The automatic-interpretation scores use GPT-4 explanations and GPT-3.5 simulations; no independent validation of that scoring procedure is reported here.
record.rows_left_out: The post references top-only MLP results (Figure 2) and reports PCA/ICA comparisons, but the supplied text gives no qualitative outcome for the top-only MLP plot and no plotted values; these were not entered as separate rows. No numerical values from any figure could be extracted.

untested.parts: No toy networks, no superposition geometry, no sparsity transition.
No test of capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Tests only one 70M model, one dictionary per site, 40-150 features, interpretability by auto-interp. It does not directly measure the spread of features across neurons.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity of dictionary features.
No comparison of 1-D with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: PCA and ICA directions in the MLP do not outperform the neuron basis. Only the first ~30 of 2048 principal components are highly interpretable. This is a baseline comparison relevant to whether the advantage is specific to sparse dictionaries.
Top-only MLP results (Figure 2) are referenced but have no stated outcome in the text.
An example learned MLP feature (currency/dollar sign) scores 0.38 on top-and-random. This is the only numeric score in the text.

record.verdict_notes: No figure values are available, so all rows rest on qualitative statements. This is an Alignment Forum post, not peer reviewed. Interpretability is scored by GPT-4 explanations and GPT-3.5 simulation. Superiority of sparse-coding directions is indirect evidence for V4 via interpretability, not a direct test of sparsity or superposition.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks, the number or sparsity of represented features, overlap geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests sparse-coding directions using interpretability scores in one model, not feature spread across neurons directly or SAE feature recovery.
Does not test whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical units; agreement of selected features across dictionaries is used for a subgroup comparison.
Uses scalar-valued features defined by directions, but does not compare one-dimensional features against multidimensional features.
